newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Parched West Europe gets rain, for now.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Parched West Europe gets rain, for now.

text.p: After months of dry weather, western Europe faces a rainswept weekend.
Anxious Britons hoped that the rain might persist and mean fewer restrictions on water use this summer. But in parts of southern England curbs put in place a year ago are still in place.

As the nation adapted to consequences of its driest 24 months for 200 years, new rules took effect that entitle people to compensation from water companies for household supply cuts forced by a drought.
In France limits on the amount of water farmers may use for irrigation were extended to the central Cher and Indre regions.
The prolonged dry spell in much of western Europe has raised fears of crop damage and helped drive world wheat prices to 1997 highs around $4.25 per bushel in Chicago futures pits.
The European Union imposed an export tax on Thursday to curb wheat exports and thereby keep a lid on internal prices.
Beyond the weekend, forecasters will so far only say that rain in the first half of May is possible. They advise against placing too much faith in forecasts for beyond the usual five days.

Western France had light rain on Friday and more is coming over the next four days, Meteo France said. And Britain is not likely to get another clear day until Wednesday, according to the Meteorological Office.
Germany too is expecting rain, although it has not suffered such a severe shortage of moisture. Spain started the change in weather, with three days of rain ending a long dry spell.
In Spain it was just in time for hard pressed farmers.
"The rain arrived at a critical point and it saved the situation, which was becoming grave," Eduardo Garcia, a technical expert at a farmers' association in the Castille Leon region, said.
But French forecasters were less sure that the scattered showers would be enough to help developing cereals crops.
And the British, hoping for substantial rainfall to replenish reservoirs run down by the driest 24 months since March 1749 to 1751, were still watching and hoping.
Rain continued in many parts of south and eastern England, the neediest areas, through Friday.
The weather has been a problem elsewhere, with Hungarian analysts complaining that it is too cold for crops to develop. German crops too have suffered from low temperatures.

And south eastern Europe has just the opposite problem to the west. Heavy rainfalls in recent weeks have flooded tens of thousands of hectares of Romanian cropland and delayed sowing, the agriculture ministry said on Wednesday.
